paragraphs: Most people regard small social lies, such as praising a mediocre meal, as harmless, even kind. Yet the practice has a cost that is easy to overlook. When praise is handed out freely, it loses its value as information, and a host who has heard 'delicious' from every guest will have no way of telling which dishes truly pleased. The effect is gradual; no single compliment does damage. Defenders of the practice reply that people understand the convention and discount accordingly, so that no one is actually deceived. This may be right, but it concedes the point at issue: if listeners must discount, then the compliment has already ceased to carry the message it appears to carry.
